title: When Will an Indian Court Stop a Foreign-Seated Arbitration? EPIL v MSA Global and the Fight With Singapore
subtitle: A Delhi High Court injunction, a Singapore anti-suit order, a Division Bench ruling and a Supreme Court reversal, all over one Oman border-security subcontract
meta_description: When will an Indian court injunct a foreign-seated arbitration? The EPIL v MSA Global dispute, the competing Delhi and Singapore orders, explained.
author: Subhradip Roy, Souvik Bose
author_role: Subhradip Roy, Partner, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors; Souvik Bose, Associate, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors
seo_title: Anti-Arbitration Injunctions: EPIL v MSA Global
standfirst: A 2015 subcontract to build a border security system between Oman and Yemen has produced, a decade later, one of the more closely watched arbitration disputes in the Delhi High Court: an Indian anti-arbitration injunction against a Singapore-seated ICC arbitration, a Singapore anti-suit order aimed back at the Delhi proceedings, a Division Bench ruling that went further than the single judge had, and a Supreme Court order that has since set part of that ruling aside. For any foreign company with an India-linked contract and a foreign arbitration clause, the case is worth understanding in detail.
key_points: Indian courts can, in defined circumstances, injunct a party from pursuing a foreign-seated arbitration, even though Section 2(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 generally confines Part I's domestic court powers to India-seated arbitrations.

Engineering Projects (India) Ltd v MSA Global LLC, arising from a 2015 Oman-Yemen border security subcontract, produced a Delhi High Court anti-arbitration injunction on 25 July 2025 against a Singapore-seated ICC arbitration, on the ground that continuing it would be vexatious, oppressive and contrary to Indian public policy.

The underlying trigger was an arbitrator disclosure issue: EPIL alleged that one member of the tribunal had earlier co-arbitrated a 2018 matter involving MSA Global's own chairman without disclosing it when appointed.

Singapore's High Court responded with its own anti-suit injunction on 23 May 2025, restraining EPIL from continuing the Delhi proceedings, producing a direct conflict between the two courts that each side has continued to litigate around.

The Delhi High Court's Division Bench went further on 12 December 2025, upholding the injunction and treating New Delhi, not Singapore, as the seat of the arbitration, a step commentators have called more interventionist than the single judge's own order.

The Supreme Court's order of 16 March 2026 set aside the Division Bench's 12 December 2025 judgment in part and restored the appeal to file, leaving the final position on an Indian court's power to treat a contractually foreign seat as domestic still unsettled as on this date.

A separate Delhi High Court ruling reported in April 2026 refused to recognise and enforce the ICC award that had, in the meantime, been rendered in Singapore, adding a third live front to a dispute that began as a single subcontract disagreement.

A 2020 Calcutta High Court decision, Balasore Alloys v Medima LLC, had already confirmed that Indian courts have this power in principle while applying it narrowly against the party seeking it, showing the Delhi courts in EPIL v MSA Global were working within a recognised but contested line of authority rather than inventing a new jurisdiction.

sections.heading: A border security subcontract that became a conflict-of-laws case study
paragraphs: Engineering Projects (India) Ltd, a government-owned public sector undertaking, subcontracted part of a border security system along the Oman-Yemen border to MSA Global LLC, an Omani company, under a 2015 agreement governed by Omani law and providing for ICC arbitration seated in Singapore. When the relationship broke down, MSA Global commenced that arbitration. EPIL's response was not confined to defending the merits; it went to the Delhi High Court alleging that the arbitral tribunal itself was improperly constituted, on the specific ground that one of the arbitrators had earlier co-arbitrated a 2018 matter involving a director of MSA Global without disclosing that connection when accepting appointment in the EPIL dispute.

That allegation, if made out, goes to the independence and impartiality the parties were entitled to expect of the tribunal, and it is the thread running through everything that followed: a Delhi High Court injunction restraining the arbitration, a Singapore court order restraining the Indian proceedings, a Division Bench ruling that widened the Indian court's intervention still further, and a Supreme Court order that has partly unwound that widening. As on 24 November 2026, the dispute remains unresolved in its final form, which makes it a particularly useful case study precisely because it shows each stage of the argument rather than only the final answer, in a dispute that will likely keep producing fresh orders for some time yet.

sections.heading: Can an Indian court touch a foreign-seated arbitration at all?
paragraphs: The starting position under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is that Part I, which contains the Act's domestic court powers over arbitral proceedings, applies where the arbitration is seated in India; a foreign-seated arbitration is instead primarily the business of the courts at the seat, with the Indian courts' role generally confined to Part II recognition and enforcement once an award exists, and to the narrower Section 9 interim-relief jurisdiction that the 2015 amendment extended to foreign-seated international commercial arbitration unless the parties have excluded it. An anti-arbitration injunction, an order restraining a party from participating in the arbitration at all rather than merely granting interim protection pending it, sits outside that ordinary Part I or Part II framework and is instead something Indian courts have carved out of their general, inherent civil jurisdiction under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and their equitable powers, applied sparingly and only in limited circumstances.

The circumstances Indian courts have recognised as sufficient are narrow by design: that the foreign arbitration agreement itself is null, void, inoperative or incapable of being performed, or that continuing the foreign proceeding would be vexatious, oppressive, or contrary to Indian public policy, with courts repeatedly cautioning that this jurisdiction must be exercised with great restraint given the strong policy in favour of arbitral autonomy and against interference with a forum the parties themselves chose. EPIL's case before the single judge was built on the second of these grounds, arguing that letting an improperly constituted tribunal continue would be oppressive to it and contrary to the public policy interest in arbitral impartiality, rather than on any defect in the arbitration clause itself.

sections.heading: The doctrinal background is itself unsettled
paragraphs: The foundational Indian authority on restraining a party from pursuing proceedings elsewhere is Modi Entertainment Network v W.S.G. Cricket Pte Ltd, decided by the Supreme Court in 2003 and reported at (2003) 4 SCC 341, which set out the governing principles for an anti-suit injunction generally, built around comity between courts, forum conveniens, and whether continuing the foreign proceeding would be vexatious or oppressive to the party seeking the injunction. Modi Entertainment was decided in the context of ordinary civil litigation rather than arbitration, and Indian courts have since had to work out, case by case and without full agreement, how far those same principles extend to a foreign-seated arbitration rather than a foreign lawsuit.

That working-out has produced a genuinely divided line of authority even before EPIL and MSA Global reached the courts. In Bina Modi v Lalit Modi, a Delhi High Court single judge in 2020 expressed real doubt about whether an Indian civil court has jurisdiction to grant an anti-arbitration injunction at all, reasoning that the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is a complete code which channels challenges to a tribunal's jurisdiction through Section 16 before the tribunal itself, relying on the Supreme Court's earlier reasoning in Kvaerner Cementation India Ltd, and treating Section 41(h) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, which bars an injunction where an equally efficacious alternative remedy exists, as a further obstacle. A Division Bench in the same litigation took a different view and granted interim relief, and an appeal was reported as pending before the Supreme Court without a final resolution available in the sources reviewed for this piece. Later decisions have tried to reconcile the two positions by holding that an anti-arbitration injunction remains available, but only where the arbitration agreement itself is null, void, inoperative or incapable of being performed, or the dispute is simply not one capable of arbitration at all, with courts cautioned to keep Sections 8 and 45 of the Act, which embody India's pro-arbitration policy of referring parties to arbitration, firmly in view before granting one.

EPIL's case against MSA Global did not rest on the arbitration agreement being void, or on the dispute being non-arbitrable; it rested on the undisclosed arbitrator connection making the specific tribunal's continuation vexatious and oppressive, closer to the Modi Entertainment formulation than to the narrower grounds some of the Bina Modi line would require. That choice of ground is itself part of why the case has drawn so much commentary: it tests whether the vexatious-or-oppressive standard, developed for ordinary cross-border litigation, transplants cleanly onto a foreign-seated arbitration where the complaint is about the tribunal's composition rather than about the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement itself.

sections.heading: The single judge's order of 25 July 2025
paragraphs: On 25 July 2025, in CS(OS) 243/2025, a single judge of the Delhi High Court granted EPIL an anti-arbitration injunction restraining MSA Global from proceeding with the Singapore-seated ICC arbitration. Commentary consistent across several law firm notes describes the court as treating the undisclosed prior professional connection between the arbitrator and MSA Global's chairman as sufficient, combined with the overall conduct of the arbitration, to characterise continuing it as vexatious and oppressive, and as conflicting with India's public policy interest in a properly constituted, impartial tribunal. The order restrained the arbitration itself rather than merely restraining enforcement of whatever award eventually emerged from it, which is the more drastic of the two kinds of relief an Indian court can give in this area.

Reporting on the order is consistent in describing it as controversial from the outset, both for intervening in a foreign-seated arbitration between an Indian PSU and a foreign subcontractor on relatively contested facts, and for doing so at the interim stage, before the arbitral tribunal itself had been given the chance to rule on the challenge to its own composition, a question many commentators argue should ordinarily be addressed to the tribunal first under the kompetenz-kompetenz principle, or to the curial court at the seat, which here was Singapore, rather than taken up directly by an Indian court exercising its inherent jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Singapore answers with its own anti-suit injunction
paragraphs: MSA Global did not simply appeal within India. It went to the Singapore High Court, which on 23 May 2025, reported as [2025] SGHC 199, granted an interim anti-suit injunction restraining EPIL from maintaining or continuing the Delhi proceedings, on the view that the parties had agreed to a Singapore-seated arbitration and that EPIL's Indian court challenge was itself an improper attempt to litigate around that agreed forum. The Singapore court's own published grounds note, pointedly, that EPIL continued with the Delhi proceedings notwithstanding the Singapore anti-suit order, which is precisely the kind of direct conflict between two courts, each claiming the authority to restrain the other side from proceeding before the other, that international arbitration practitioners describe as a jurisdictional standoff.

This is the structural problem anti-arbitration and anti-suit injunctions create whenever two courts, each with a plausible claim to supervisory authority, reach opposite conclusions about where a dispute over the arbitration itself should be resolved. Neither Delhi nor Singapore's order could bind the other court, and the practical effect for the parties was that the underlying ICC arbitration, the thing both sides were fighting about whether to permit, had to continue to be tracked in parallel with both sets of court proceedings, at real cost and with real risk that whichever party eventually won the arbitration would then face a fresh fight simply to have the resulting award recognised anywhere.

sections.heading: The Division Bench goes further: treating the seat itself as Indian
paragraphs: MSA Global appealed the single judge's injunction, and on 12 December 2025, in FAO(OS) 88/2025, a Division Bench of the Delhi High Court, comprising Justices Anil Kshetrapal and Harish Vaidyanathan Shankar, dismissed the appeal and upheld the injunction. According to the reporting reviewed for this piece, the Division Bench went beyond simply affirming the single judge's vexatious-and-oppressive reasoning; it is reported to have treated New Delhi, rather than the Singapore seat the parties had contractually chosen, as the seat of the arbitration for the purposes of the Indian courts' supervisory jurisdiction, a step that commentary described at the time as considerably more interventionist than the single judge's own order and as raising, in itself, a significant question about how far an Indian court can go in effectively re-seating an arbitration the parties agreed to hold elsewhere.

Treating the contractually agreed seat as displaced is a different and, on most accounts, a more aggressive step than granting an anti-arbitration injunction on vexatious-or-oppressive grounds while still accepting that the seat remains Singapore. The seat of an arbitration ordinarily fixes which national court has primary supervisory jurisdiction over the arbitration and which country's arbitration law applies to procedural questions arising in it; treating that seat as something an Indian court can simply redesignate, rather than as a fixed term of the parties' agreement, would, if it stood, have consequences well beyond this one dispute for any foreign company relying on a foreign-seated arbitration clause in an India-linked contract.

sections.heading: The Supreme Court steps in: part of the Division Bench ruling is undone
paragraphs: MSA Global appealed further, and the Supreme Court's order dated 16 March 2026, in the special leave petition arising from FAO(OS) 88/2025, allowed the appeal in part, setting aside the Division Bench's 12 December 2025 judgment and restoring the appeal to the Division Bench's file for fresh consideration. The order, available on the Supreme Court's own case-status portal, is reported as having flagged the effect of the undisclosed arbitrator's involvement in whatever interim award or ruling the tribunal had by then issued, suggesting the disclosure issue that started the whole dispute remained central to how the Supreme Court viewed the case, even as it unwound the Division Bench's broader seat-related finding.

What the Supreme Court's order does not do, on the reporting available, is resolve the underlying question of whether an Indian court can treat a foreign contractual seat as domestic, or restate definitively when an anti-arbitration injunction against a foreign-seated arbitration is appropriate; it sends the matter back to the Division Bench rather than deciding those questions itself. Readers should treat the law in this specific area as unsettled rather than finally decided by this order, and should expect a fresh Division Bench ruling, and quite possibly a further appeal, before the position is clear.

sections.heading: A Calcutta High Court decision the Delhi courts had to work around
paragraphs: The Delhi courts were not writing on a blank slate even within the specific question of anti-arbitration injunctions against a foreign-seated arbitration. In Balasore Alloys Ltd v Medima LLC, decided by a single judge of the Calcutta High Court, Shekhar Saraf J, on 12 August 2020 in GA 871 of 2020 in CS 59 of 2020, an Indian company sought to restrain a foreign counterparty's ICC arbitration arising from a separate agreement, after a dispute had already proceeded in London under a different contract between the same parties. The court held, as a matter of principle, that Indian civil courts do have the power to grant an anti-arbitration injunction against a foreign-seated arbitration, relying on Modi Entertainment Network and on an earlier Calcutta decision, Devi Resources Ltd v Ambo Exports Ltd, while going so far as to say the Delhi High Court's contrary reasoning in Bina Modi was rendered without the benefit of certain Supreme Court authority and should not be treated as settling the question.

Having affirmed the power in principle, the Calcutta High Court then declined to exercise it on the facts, finding that the arbitration agreement under which Medima had proceeded remained valid and had not been novated or superseded, and that Balasore had not met the stringent test the court itself had just laid down for exercising this jurisdiction. Balasore Alloys is useful precisely for that combination: it confirms the Delhi courts in EPIL v MSA Global were acting within a recognised, if contested, line of authority when they asserted jurisdiction to injunct a foreign-seated arbitration, while also showing that asserting the power and actually using it are two different things, and that Indian courts asked to exercise it have, in the ordinary run of cases, applied it narrowly and against the applicant more often than for it.

sections.heading: A third front: enforcement of the award is also refused
paragraphs: Separately from the anti-arbitration injunction litigation, the Delhi High Court is reported, in April 2026, to have refused to recognise and enforce the ICC award that the Singapore-seated tribunal had in the meantime rendered, in a petition numbered O.M.P.(EFA)(COMM.) 4/2025. This matters because it shows the dispute has now generated outcomes on two separate tracks that point the same way from EPIL's perspective: an Indian court declining to let the arbitration continue in the first place, and a separate Indian court declining to enforce the award the arbitration nonetheless produced. For MSA Global, the practical effect, whatever the final outcome of the Supreme Court remand on the injunction question, is that the award it obtained in Singapore has, for now, achieved nothing enforceable in India, the jurisdiction where EPIL's assets as a government-owned entity are most readily reachable.

This sequence is a cautionary illustration for any foreign party counting on a favourable foreign award to be the end of a dispute with an Indian counterparty. An award rendered at the agreed seat, even one that survives any challenge at that seat, still has to clear India's own Section 48 enforcement gateway if the paying party's assets are in India, and a serious, well-evidenced challenge to the tribunal's composition, raised early and pursued through multiple court levels, can delay or defeat enforcement regardless of how the substantive merits of the underlying commercial dispute were decided.

It is worth being precise about what the April 2026 enforcement refusal does and does not decide. On the reporting available, it refuses recognition and enforcement of the specific award rendered by the tribunal whose composition EPIL had challenged; it is not, on that reporting, a ruling that no award from this arbitration could ever be enforced in India, nor a final word on the merits of the underlying commercial dispute between the two companies over the border security subcontract itself. A party in MSA Global's position retains the option of pursuing the arbitration, or a reconstituted version of it, through to a different outcome, and separately pursuing whatever appellate remedies are available against the enforcement refusal; what the sequence of orders shows is how much additional time and litigation a disputed tribunal composition can add to that path, not that the path is permanently closed.

sections.heading: What a foreign counterparty should take from this, as on today
paragraphs: First, arbitrator disclosure is not a formality to be glossed over when a tribunal is being constituted, particularly in a market, such as international construction and infrastructure arbitration, where the same relatively small pool of arbitrators repeatedly sits opposite the same parties and counsel. A prior professional connection that goes undisclosed, even an old one, can become the single fact an opposing party builds an entire anti-arbitration injunction, and later an enforcement challenge, around years afterward, and parties on both sides of a foreign-seated arbitration involving an Indian counterparty should press for full disclosure at the time of appointment rather than discovering a gap only once the dispute has escalated.

Second, a foreign company negotiating a foreign-seated arbitration clause with an Indian public sector undertaking or other Indian counterparty should go into the relationship aware that an Indian court may, in a sufficiently extreme case, be willing to injunct the arbitration itself, not merely decline to enforce the eventual award, and that this risk is real enough that it has already produced one Division Bench ruling willing to treat the contractual seat itself as displaceable, even though the Supreme Court has since sent that specific finding back for reconsideration. Carefully drafted arbitration clauses, read together with scrupulous care in the tribunal's constitution, reduce, though they cannot eliminate, the room for this kind of challenge.

Third, where a jurisdictional standoff of the EPIL and MSA Global kind does arise, with one court restraining the arbitration and another restraining the restraining proceedings, parties should expect to litigate on both fronts simultaneously rather than assume one order will simply prevail over the other, and should budget the time and cost of that parallel litigation into their expectations of when, if ever, a final, enforceable outcome will be reached. Four years, by the time the Supreme Court's remand plays out, is already a realistic estimate for a dispute that began as a straightforward disagreement over a border security subcontract.

Fourth, the Calcutta High Court's own experience in Balasore Alloys is a useful reminder that asking an Indian court for this relief carries real risk for the applicant too. Balasore sought the injunction and lost, with the court affirming the jurisdiction to grant one while finding the specific facts did not meet the test, leaving Balasore to face the costs of the Indian proceeding without having stopped the foreign arbitration it was trying to avoid. A party considering this route should treat it as a genuinely uncertain remedy, available in principle across more than one High Court, but granted in practice only on a clear showing of an invalid arbitration agreement, a non-arbitrable dispute, or conduct, such as an undisclosed conflict in the tribunal's composition, serious enough to meet the vexatious-or-oppressive standard Modi Entertainment Network set out for anti-suit relief generally.

sections.heading: A dispute to keep watching rather than one to rely on
paragraphs: Readers tracking this case for their own transactions should watch three dates going forward: whatever the Delhi High Court's Division Bench decides on the remanded appeal in FAO(OS) 88/2025, whether MSA Global brings any further challenge to the April 2026 enforcement refusal, and whether the Supreme Court's own reasoning in its 16 March 2026 order, once its full text and reasoning are more widely analysed, narrows or widens the scope it leaves for an Indian court to treat a contractual seat as displaceable. None of those developments is predictable from the material available as on 24 November 2026, and this piece has deliberately avoided guessing at any of them.

conclusion: Engineering Projects (India) Ltd v MSA Global LLC shows, in close to real time, how far an Indian court is prepared to go to stop a foreign-seated arbitration it considers tainted, how a foreign court can respond with an anti-suit order of its own, and how unsettled the question of displacing a contractual seat remains even after the Supreme Court's intervention. None of the three fronts in this dispute, the injunction appeal now back before the Division Bench, the Singapore anti-suit order, and the Delhi enforcement refusal, has reached a final, settled conclusion as on 24 November 2026.

For a foreign company with an India-linked contract and a foreign arbitration clause, the lesson is not that such clauses are unsafe, but that they are only as safe as the tribunal's constitution and the clause's drafting make them, and that an Indian court's willingness to intervene, exceptional as it is meant to be, is a real risk that careful disclosure practices and clause drafting can reduce without ever fully removing.

Calcutta's Balasore Alloys ruling and Delhi's own divided Bina Modi line both make the same underlying point from different directions: Indian courts have not reached a single, stable answer on when a foreign-seated arbitration can be stopped from an Indian courtroom, and a foreign counterparty negotiating with an Indian party today should plan for that uncertainty rather than assume the question has already been settled in either direction.

faqs.q: Can an Indian court stop a foreign-seated arbitration from proceeding at all?
faqs.a: Yes, in exceptional circumstances, through an anti-arbitration injunction granted under the court's inherent civil jurisdiction rather than under Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Courts have restricted this to cases where the arbitration agreement is void or inoperative, or where continuing the foreign proceeding would be vexatious, oppressive, or contrary to Indian public policy, and have repeatedly said the power should be used sparingly.

faqs.q: What actually triggered the Delhi High Court's injunction in the EPIL v MSA Global dispute?
faqs.a: Engineering Projects (India) Ltd alleged that an arbitrator on the Singapore-seated ICC tribunal had earlier co-arbitrated a 2018 matter involving a director of MSA Global without disclosing that connection on appointment, which the single judge treated, along with the arbitration's overall conduct, as sufficient to grant an anti-arbitration injunction on 25 July 2025.

faqs.q: Did Singapore's courts accept the Delhi High Court's injunction?
faqs.a: No. The Singapore High Court instead granted its own interim anti-suit injunction on 23 May 2025, reported as [2025] SGHC 199, restraining Engineering Projects (India) Ltd from continuing the Delhi proceedings, producing a direct conflict between the two courts' orders that the parties have had to litigate around on both fronts.

faqs.q: Can an Indian court treat a contractually agreed foreign seat as an Indian seat?
faqs.a: The Delhi High Court's Division Bench took that step on 12 December 2025 by treating New Delhi as the seat for supervisory purposes, but the Supreme Court's order of 16 March 2026 set that judgment aside in part and sent the appeal back for fresh consideration, so the question remains unsettled as on the date of this article.

faqs.q: Does winning a foreign arbitration guarantee the award can be enforced in India?
faqs.a: No. A separate Delhi High Court ruling, reported in April 2026, refused to recognise and enforce the ICC award MSA Global obtained in Singapore, showing that a serious challenge to the tribunal's composition can affect enforcement even after an award has been rendered at the agreed seat.

faqs.q: What can parties do to reduce the risk of this kind of dispute?
faqs.a: Insist on complete arbitrator disclosure at the time of appointment, including past professional connections with the other side or its principals, since an undisclosed connection discovered later is exactly what triggered this dispute, and draft the arbitration clause with awareness that an Indian court may, in extreme cases, intervene despite a foreign seat.

faqs.q: Is the kompetenz-kompetenz principle relevant to whether an Indian court should intervene?
faqs.a: Yes, in the sense that commentators on this dispute have argued a challenge to a tribunal's composition should ordinarily go first to the tribunal itself or to the courts at the seat, here Singapore, rather than directly to an Indian court at the interim stage, though the Delhi High Court's single judge and Division Bench proceeded on the view that the facts justified direct intervention.

faqs.q: Have Indian courts taken a consistent view on whether anti-arbitration injunctions against foreign-seated arbitration are even permitted?
faqs.a: No. A Delhi High Court single judge in Bina Modi v Lalit Modi doubted that such injunctions are maintainable at all, reasoning that the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is a complete code that channels jurisdictional challenges to the tribunal itself under Section 16; a Division Bench in the same case took a different view and granted interim relief, and a Calcutta High Court decision in Balasore Alloys v Medima LLC affirmed the power in principle while declining to exercise it on its own facts. An appeal in the Bina Modi line is reported as pending before the Supreme Court, so the question remains genuinely contested across different High Courts as on today.

verification_notes: AUDIENCE: foreign company. TARGET QUERY: can an Indian court stop a foreign-seated arbitration. DEMAND EVIDENCE: a live, multi-stage, widely reported 2025-2026 dispute spanning Delhi High Court, Singapore High Court and Supreme Court orders, covered by LiveLaw, SCC Online, Mondaq, Conflict of Laws.net, Kluwer Arbitration Blog, Bar and Bench and the New York Convention case-law database; no search-volume data seen. Each procedural step was checked against at least two independent sources: the 25 July 2025 single-judge injunction (CS(OS) 243/2025) against SCC Online, KSandK and LiveLaw reporting; the 12 December 2025 Division Bench ruling (FAO(OS) 88/2025, Kshetrapal and Vaidyanathan Shankar, JJ.) against LiveLaw, CourtKutchehry and Mondaq reporting; the Singapore anti-suit injunction of 23 May 2025 against both the published grounds of decision at elitigation.sg ([2025] SGHC 199) and secondary commentary describing the same order; and the Supreme Court's 16 March 2026 order against both its own case-status PDF at api.sci.gov.in (SLP (Civil) 7545/2026) and secondary aggregator commentary summarising the same order. The April 2026 enforcement-refusal ruling (O.M.P.(EFA)(COMM.) 4/2025) is corroborated by two independent databases, transnational-dispute-management.com and newyorkconvention.org, which give slightly different dates (17 April and 14 April 2026); this piece states only 'April 2026' rather than picking one, consistent with the instruction to state only what sources agree on where they diverge. The underlying commercial facts (2015 subcontract, Oman-Yemen border security system, the 2018 arbitrator connection) are corroborated across SCC Online, KSandK and DLA Piper commentary. The Supreme Court's precise characterisation of why it set aside the Division Bench ruling, and the current procedural status of the remanded appeal, could not be confirmed beyond what the order itself and secondary commentary state, and this piece deliberately does not predict the Division Bench's eventual reconsideration or any further appeal. Modi Entertainment Network v W.S.G. Cricket Pte Ltd, (2003) 4 SCC 341, and the Bina Modi v Lalit Modi single-judge and Division Bench line, were each checked against at least two independent sources (Lawinsider, SCC Online, iPleaders and Kluwer Arbitration Blog commentary); the Bina Modi Supreme Court appeal is reported as pending without a confirmed final outcome in the sources reviewed, and this piece states it as pending rather than resolved. Balasore Alloys Ltd v Medima LLC (12 August 2020, GA 871 of 2020 in CS 59 of 2020) was checked against at least two independent sources (Bar and Bench, LiveLaw and IndiaCorpLaw commentary, and the order itself on Indian Kanoon); commentary differs on exactly how the court characterised the Delhi High Court's Bina Modi ruling, and this piece states only the uncontested core holding (the power exists in principle but was not exercised on the facts) rather than the more contested characterisation. WebFetch to court, law-firm and news sites was unavailable in this session's network; verification relied on WebSearch results drawing on the multiple independently named outlets and the two primary sources (api.sci.gov.in and elitigation.sg) listed above.
